idiom_name: clone operation on a self-copying prototype (+ optional prototype registry)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give every prototype type a clone operation that returns an independent object of the same dynamic type and keeps construction knowledge inside the class, so clients ask the prototype to clone itself instead of naming a class. Decide per field whether it is copied by value, deep-copied or shared (immutable state, flyweights, handles) and document that decision; deep-copying a graph needs an identity map so cycles and shared references stay shared in the copy. Where several configured prototypes exist, keep them in a registry keyed by name and clone the registered exemplar rather than re-creating it, treating registry entries as read-only templates. Constructor and clone must not diverge: implement clone through a copy constructor or a factory so construction stays in one place. Prefer typed, named copy methods (clone(): this, copy(), DeepClone(), with(preset)) over generic object-returning cloning in public APIs. Treat prototype registry entries as immutable templates and synchronise or freeze registry updates if prototypes can be added at run time.
pitfalls: A clone that copies fields only shallowly leaves mutable substructures shared; callers who mutate the copy silently mutate the original.
Deep copy without a visited/identity map loops on cycles or duplicates nodes that the original shared.
Copying state that carries identity or resources (ids, listeners, locks, file handles) instead of re-initialising or deliberately sharing it.
Letting client code keep constructing concrete products (new Circle(...) next to clone()) recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
Over-cloning large object graphs when only a small subset is needed; profile before applying the pattern broadly.
Mutating a shared prototype registry entry, causing all subsequent clones to inherit unexpected state.

Wrong move: treat clone() as constructor-equivalent -> constructor-only validation, identity assignment or dependency registration may not run -> instead reset identity-bearing state and invoke explicit post-clone validation/initialization.

Wrong move: clone an object that owns sockets, locks or other external resources -> the copy aliases or duplicates ownership and breaks lifecycle guarantees -> instead clone copyable configuration and inject or recreate resources.
